name: Compression vs Strangle
keyCorrections: If you feel sharp pain in a muscle belly (calf, bicep): you are in a compression lock — tap if the pain escalates past your comfort level
If you feel pressure on the sides of your neck (carotids): you are in a blood choke — defend, escape, or reset
If you feel pressure on your chin, throat, or back of the head: tap immediately — you are in a crank or air choke
description: Recognize compression locks (calf slicer, bicep slicer) vs strangles and respond correctly: tap when compression targets the joint, fight when targeting the neck. Knowing the difference prevents panic tapping to safe techniques and dangerous delay on dangerous ones.
shortInstruction: Compression attacks the muscle against the bone (tap when pain is sharp), strangles attack the neck (fight if blood choke, tap if air choke or crank). If unsure, tap — muscle damage takes weeks to heal.
summary: Compression attacks (slicers) apply pressure that traps a muscle belly against a bone, creating sharp localized pain. Strangles (blood chokes) apply pressure to the carotid arteries. The response is opposite: for compression locks, tap when the pain becomes sharp (they will not make you unconscious). For blood chokes, you can defend longer because unconsciousness is reversible. The danger is confusing a deep blood choke that feels like neck pressure with a crank — tap early if the pressure feels wrong.
whyItWorks: Compression locks do not cause unconsciousness — they cause muscle and nerve compression pain that increases gradually
Blood chokes cause unconsciousness in 4-10 seconds — you have time to defend but must recognize the threat level
Air chokes (trachea pressure) and neck cranks (spine pressure) require immediate tapping due to structural injury risk
Knowing which type of attack you are in determines whether you should fight, escape, or tap immediately
commonMistakes: Panic tapping to compression locks that are not fully applied — compression pain is sharp but rarely causes lasting damage if you tap early
Not tapping early enough to air chokes or neck cranks — 'toughing out' a trachea choke can cause vocal cord damage
Confusing a tight blood choke with a neck crank — a blood choke applies pressure to the sides of the neck, not the front or back
Fighting a compression lock too long — muscle damage from slicers can take weeks to heal
safetySummary: Calf slicers compress the gastrocnemius against the tibia — painful but rarely causes structural damage if you tap when pain becomes sharp
Bicep slicers compress the biceps brachii against the humerus — can cause nerve damage if held too long
Wrist slicers (from certain lapel or grip positions) can compress median and ulnar nerves — tap early
Blood chokes that are held past unconsciousness can cause seizures or, in rare cases, stroke — always release immediately on tap or limp body
Air chokes (pressure on the trachea) can cause vocal cord damage, thyroid cartilage fracture, or breathing difficulty — tap immediately

systemLogic.corePrinciple: The three attack types on the neck/limbs require different responses: Compression Lock → tap on sharp pain. Blood Choke → defend/escape with time. Air Choke / Neck Crank → tap immediately.

decisionTree.condition: Compression locks (slicers): the attacking limb (shin, forearm) drives the muscle belly against the bone, creating ischemia (lack of blood flow) and nerve compression. The pain increases gradually
decisionTree.action: you have time to tap. Do not 'tough out' compression locks as they can cause rhabdomyolysis (muscle tissue breakdown) in extreme cases

Blood chokes (strangles): the attacking arm(s) compress the carotid arteries, preventing oxygenated blood from reaching the brain. You have 4-10 seconds of consciousness after the choke is locked. Blood chokes are safe to train because unconsciousness is reversible
Air chokes: pressure on the trachea/windpipe restricts breathing. These can damage the hyoid bone, thyroid cartilage, and vocal cords. Tap immediately on trachea pressure
Neck cranks: leverage the cervical spine through the chin, back of the head, or base of skull. Can cause disc herniation, ligament damage, and chronic neck pain. Tap immediately

moneyDetails: Knowing the difference between compression, blood choke, and neck crank is essential for safe training — incorrect responses lead to injury or unnecessary tapping
The ability to distinguish attack types in real time separates experienced grapplers from beginners
Understanding when to fight (blood choke) and when to tap (crank/air choke/compression pain) optimizes your defensive decisions in competition
fixItFast: If you are unsure what type of attack you are in: check where the pressure is — sides of neck = blood choke, front of neck = air choke, chin/spine = crank, muscle belly = compression
If the opponent has a compression lock but you are comfortable: tap when the pain becomes sharp — do not wait for structural damage
If you feel any neck pressure that seems 'wrong': tap. Your instinct is usually correct
